title: Military (24-hour) time
blurb: Convert between standard a.m./p.m. time and four-digit military time in both directions, including the noon and midnight hours, and put times from a whole day in order.
question: One dose of a medication is charted at 0040 and another at 1240. In standard time, when was each dose given?

teach.body: Formally, military (24-hour) time numbers the hours of a day from 00 to 23 and writes every time as four digits with no colon and no a.m. or p.m.: the first two digits are the hour, the last two the minutes. In plain English: instead of counting to 12 twice, you keep counting after noon, so 1 p.m. becomes 13 hundred. Hospitals use it so that 7:00 can never be mistaken for the wrong half of the day.

1. Midnight hour (12:00 to 12:59 a.m.): write 00 for the hour, so 12:30 a.m. = 0030. 2. 1:00 to 11:59 a.m.: keep the hour and add a leading zero if needed, so 7:05 a.m. = 0705. 3. Noon hour (12:00 to 12:59 p.m.): write it as it is, so 12:45 p.m. = 1245. 4. 1:00 to 11:59 p.m.: add 12 to the hour, so 6:40 p.m. = 1840.

teach.caption: The two 12 o'clock hours are the exceptions: 12 a.m. becomes 00, and 12 p.m. stays 12.

teach.caption: The minutes never change: only the hour digits and the a.m. or p.m. label do.

items: 4:20 p.m. to military: p.m. and not 12, so 4 + 12 = 16. Answer: 1620. Check: 16 - 12 = 4, p.m.
12:50 a.m. to military: the midnight hour is 00. Answer: 0050. Check: 00 means 12, a.m.
12:05 p.m. to military: the noon hour stays 12. Answer: 1205. Check: hour 12 is p.m.
2115 to standard: 21 - 12 = 9, p.m. Answer: 9:15 p.m. Check: 9 + 12 = 21.
0608 to standard: hour 06 is a.m. Answer: 6:08 a.m. Check: 6:08 a.m. keeps its zero as 0608.

teach.caption: These two hours cause most military-time errors: learn them as a pair.

teach.h: Scenario: Daniela checks a medication record
teach.body: Daniela, an LPN applying to an RN bridge program, sees doses charted at 0040 and 1240. Hour 00 is the midnight hour, so 0040 is 12:40 a.m., just after midnight. Hour 12 is the noon hour, so 1240 is 12:40 p.m. The doses are 12 hours apart. Had she subtracted 12 from 1240, she would have written "0:40 p.m.", a time that does not exist.

teach.text: The classic slips: adding 12 to a noon-hour time (12:45 p.m. written as 2445), writing midnight as 1200 and noon as 0000, adding 12 to a morning time, forgetting to add 12 to a p.m. time, and dropping the leading zero (0905 written as 905). Military time is always four digits.

items: Four digits, no colon, no a.m. or p.m.: hours 00 to 23, then minutes.
1:00 to 11:59 p.m.: add 12 to the hour. 13 to 23: subtract 12 and write p.m.
Morning hours keep their leading zero: 7:05 a.m. = 0705.
To order times from one day, convert them all to military time and compare the numbers.

summary: You can now write any standard time as a four-digit military time and read any military time back as a.m. or p.m., including the tricky noon and midnight hours. You can also put a mixed list of times from one day in order.

A.why: p.m. and not the noon hour, so add 12: 3 + 12 = 15. Answer: 1525.

whyNot.0: 0325 is 3:25 a.m.; 12 must be added to a p.m. hour.
whyNot.1: This adds 10 to the hour; 1325 is 1:25 p.m.
whyNot.3: This adds 14 to the hour; 1725 is 5:25 p.m.

A.why: Hours 13 to 23 are p.m.: 22 - 12 = 10, so 10:10 p.m.

whyNot.0: Hours after 12 are p.m.; 10:10 a.m. is 1010.
whyNot.2: This subtracts 10 instead of 12; 12:10 p.m. is 1210.
whyNot.3: This subtracts 14 instead of 12; 8:10 p.m. is 2010.

A.q: How is 12:20 a.m. written in military time?
A.why: 12:xx a.m. is the midnight hour, written 00: 0020.

whyNot.2: This adds 12 to the midnight hour; nothing is added to 12:xx a.m., which is written 00xx.

B.q: Which pair shows the same time in military and standard form?

whyNot.0: 0715 is 7:15 a.m.; p.m. hours need 12 added.
whyNot.2: 1715 is 5:15 p.m.; it adds 10 instead of 12.
whyNot.3: 1915 is 7:15 p.m.; this subtracts 10 instead of 12.

B.q: A clinic opens at 0730 and closes at 1830. In standard time, when does it open and close?

whyNot.2: This swaps a.m. and p.m.; hour 07 is morning and hour 18 is evening.
whyNot.3: Hour 18 is after noon, so 1830 is p.m., not a.m.

B.q: Which military time is the latest in the day?
B.why: 1205 is 12:05 p.m., just after noon. 1159 and 1150 are before noon, and 0045 is just after midnight.

whyNot.1: 0045 is 12:45 a.m., early in the morning.

C.q: Which list orders these times from earliest to latest in one day: 1:05 p.m., 0015, 11:40 a.m., 1300?

whyNot.1: This puts 0015 at the end of the day and 1:05 p.m. before 1300; 0015 is 12:15 a.m.
whyNot.3: 0015 is 12:15 a.m., which comes before 11:40 a.m.

C.q: A night shift runs from 7:00 p.m. to 7:30 a.m. Which pair gives the start and end in military time?

whyNot.0: This swaps the halves of the day: the shift starts in the evening (1900) and ends in the morning (0730).
whyNot.2: 1930 is 7:30 p.m.; the shift ends at 7:30 a.m., which is 0730.
whyNot.3: 0700 is 7:00 a.m.; the shift starts at 7:00 p.m., which is 1900.

C.q: A dose is due at 9:45 p.m., and the nurse gives it 20 minutes late. Which military time should be charted?

whyNot.0: 1005 is 10:05 a.m.; 12 must be added to a p.m. hour.
whyNot.1: 2145 is the scheduled time; the dose was given 20 minutes later.
whyNot.3: This carries an extra hour; 45 + 20 = 65 minutes is 1 hour 5 minutes, so only one hour is carried.

reteach.title: Think of a stopwatch started at midnight
reteach.question: If you started a stopwatch at midnight and never reset it at noon, what would it read at 3 in the afternoon?

blocks.body: A standard clock resets to 12 at noon and counts 1, 2, 3 again, so it needs a.m. and p.m. to tell the halves apart. A stopwatch started at midnight just keeps going: at 3 in the afternoon it has run 15 hours. Military time is that stopwatch. It reads 0000 at midnight, 1200 at noon, 1500 at 3 p.m., and 2359 a minute before it starts again.

blocks.text: The stopwatch has run 0 hours, not 12, during the first hour after midnight: 12:30 a.m. is 0030.

explain.body: From 1:00 to 11:59 a.m., keep the hour and minutes and write four digits, adding a leading zero for hours 1 to 9: 6:08 a.m. = 0608.

test.why: Morning hour 6 becomes 06, and the minutes stay 08: 0608.

whyNot.1: 1808 is 6:08 p.m.; 12 is added only to p.m. hours.
whyNot.2: This swaps the hour and minute digits; 0806 is 8:06 a.m.
whyNot.3: This adds 10 to the hour; 1608 is 4:08 p.m.

explain.body: From 1:00 to 11:59 p.m., add 12 to the hour: 1 p.m. = 13, 6 p.m. = 18, 10 p.m. = 22.

whyNot.0: 1050 is 10:50 a.m.; 12 must be added to a p.m. hour.
whyNot.1: This adds 10 to the hour; 2050 is 8:50 p.m.
whyNot.3: This adds 13 to the hour; 2350 is 11:50 p.m.

explain.body: 12:xx a.m. is written 00xx (0005 = 12:05 a.m.). 12:xx p.m. is written 12xx (1205 = 12:05 p.m.). Nothing is added to either.

test.why: Hour 00 is the midnight hour, so 0005 is 5 minutes after midnight: 12:05 a.m.

whyNot.2: This misreads the minutes; 05 is 5 minutes, not 50.
whyNot.3: This reads 05 as the hour; the first two digits (00) are the hour.

explain.body: Look at the first two digits. 13 to 23: subtract 12 and write p.m. 1640: 16 - 12 = 4, so 4:40 p.m.

test.why: 16 - 12 = 4, and hours after 12 are p.m.: 4:40 p.m.

whyNot.0: Hour 16 is after noon, so the time is p.m.
